title: Nichiren
hook: the monk who taught chanting the Lotus Sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo

segments.voice: Yesterday, being-time: the pine is time, the mountain is time, and so are you. Your line: you are time. When you caught yourself short of time, did you stop for one breath? Day one thousand.

Day one thousand, and today a sound. In homes and community centers, people kneel or sit before a scroll and chant one phrase, steadily, again and again, a rolling rhythm that can fill a room: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. There are no long instructions to memorize, no complicated posture. Just a phrase, a voice, and a scroll. That chant goes back to a Japanese monk who said the title of one sutra held the whole of the Buddha's teaching. Today, Nichiren.
screen: `ONE PHRASE, CHANTED.` → `NAMU MYOHO RENGE KYO.` → `A MONK WHO PICKED A TITLE.`

segments.voice: Nichiren was a monk in Japan who studied widely and came to one conviction: the Lotus Sutra was the Buddha's highest teaching, and the way into it was its title. Tradition says he first chanted the phrase aloud at his home temple, facing the sunrise. Let's open the phrase. Namu means something like devotion, or I take refuge in. Myoho is the wonderful law, or mystic law, the truth the sutra teaches. Renge is the lotus flower, which grows out of mud and blooms clean. Kyo is sutra, a teaching. Myoho Renge Kyo is the sutra's title; namu is the devotion placed in front of it. Put together: devotion to the Lotus Sutra of the wonderful law. Why a title? In Nichiren's teaching, the title isn't a label on the outside of a book. It holds the whole sutra inside it, the way a seed holds a tree. So chanting the title is a way of meeting the entire teaching with your own voice, not only with your eyes or your intellect. That makes it a practice open to anyone, not only to scholar monks. Nichiren was outspoken. He wrote that Japan's troubles came from turning away from the Lotus, he argued hard with the schools of his day, and tradition remembers that he was sent into exile for it. Today his followers belong to several groups, including Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai, and they differ on how to read his teaching and on who carries it forward. What they share is the chant. For Nichiren Buddhists, saying the title is not a warm-up for practice. It is the practice.
screen: `A MONK AND ONE SUTRA.` · `NAMU, MYOHO, RENGE, KYO.` · `THE TITLE HOLDS THE WHOLE.` · `SEVERAL GROUPS, ONE CHANT.` · then, large: `THE CHANT IS THE PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: chant the title three times, the way Nichiren Buddhists do. If saying it isn't right for you, simply listen to the sound of it in your head. Sit up. Take a breath. Then, at an easy, steady pace: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Again: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Once more: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. Now let it go quiet. Feel what the sound leaves behind, in the chest, in the throat, in the room. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Nichiren. The Japanese monk who taught that the title of the Lotus Sutra, Myoho Renge Kyo, holds the whole teaching, and that chanting Namu Myoho Renge Kyo is the practice. Today's word.
Your line: the title of the Lotus. Today, notice one title, of a book, a song, a job, and ask what whole story it might be holding. Day one thousand.

howItsDone: Nichiren Buddhists chant Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, called the daimoku, often morning and evening before a scroll called the Gohonzon, and recite passages from the Lotus Sutra; groups meet in homes and temples to chant together.

fork.setup: you're Nichiren. which part of the Lotus Sutra do you teach people to chant, as holding the whole teaching?
fork.reveal: Nichiren taught chanting namu, devotion, before the title, Myoho Renge Kyo, which holds the sutra like a seed holds the tree.

notes: The first chanting at his home temple (Seichoji) facing the sunrise is framed as tradition; confirm.
Glosses of namu, myoho, renge, kyo are standard but simplified; confirm with a Nichiren Keeper, who may prefer 'mystic law'.
The seed-and-tree image is an illustration; confirm it fits how Nichiren schools explain the daimoku.
'Sent into exile' is framed as tradition; it is well attested (Izu, Sado) but kept vague under the claims rule.
The sentence on Japan's troubles paraphrases the argument of the Rissho Ankoku Ron; confirm it is fair and not framed against other schools.
Listing Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai: check the groups are named fairly and in a neutral order.
howItsDone mentions morning and evening practice and the Gohonzon; 'many also recite passages' should be confirmed or softened.
Practice invites chanting the real daimoku three times (from the outline), with a listen-only option.
Editor: fixed the garbled review question and carry ('what a whole life it might be holding'); rewrote the fork, which repeated day 992's 'ordinary people with no time for scriptures' angle.
Auditor: the word segment and fork reveal called Namu Myoho Renge Kyo the title; the title is Myoho Renge Kyo and namu is prefixed to it. Corrected in voice and games.
